about: Building types (roadmap BT1b): types of the British Isles and their sourced 'family' links. kind: descent (grew out of), variant (a form of), influence (shaped by, without descent; also from abroad), replacement (superseded by), revival, convergence (similar form, separate origin). confidence: documented / probable / disputed (with views). fish: FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types concept id (Historic England, OGL v3.0). Checked by `python -m bidb.building_types`.

types.name: Roundhouse

period.text: Bronze Age to the sub-Roman period. The standard house of Britain and Ireland from the Bronze Age (which began c. 2500-2200 BC; the oldest documented roundhouse, in south-west Scotland, is of the 3rd millennium BC) through the Iron Age (to AD 43), and in some areas into the sub-Roman period (407-577, longer in the west); c. 600 is approximate. Modern eco-roundhouses since the late 20th century are a revival.

types.structure: walls of stone, or of wooden posts with wattle-and-daub panels, under a conical thatched roof
types.plan: circular

types.name: Broch

period.text: Iron Age; the first perhaps c. 300 BC (one claimed earlier, at Old Scatness, 390-200 BC), most built in the 1st centuries BC and AD, and broch building ending around AD 100-200.

types.structure: thick, usually hollow dry-stone walls holding galleries, cells and a stair, with a tapering profile
types.note: Where brochs came from was long disputed: mid-20th-century archaeologists saw them as the work of incomers from the south; the view now is that they developed in Scotland.

types.name: Longhouse

period.text: Medieval and early modern: one in Wales dated to the 11th century, the earliest on Dartmoor thought to be of the 13th century; built through the Middle Ages into the early modern period, and by 1700 most had been adapted, with separate buildings for livestock. No source gives the last one built.

types.name: Blackhouse

period.text: Few examples before the 18th century have been excavated, though the tradition is thought far older; still built in the late 19th century (the Arnol museum house, 1875), they were replaced by 'white houses' from the end of the 1800s, and the last were lived in until the 1970s. No source gives the last one built; 1700 and 1900 are approximate.

types.name: Wealden house

types.name: Double-pile house

period.text: Compact plans two rooms deep appear in England in the last quarter of the 16th century (Newton, Brecon, 1582, the earliest in Wales); much in vogue from the late 17th to the mid-18th century, and still built in the early 19th (Newfield Hall, Minshull Vernon). No source gives when they stopped; c. 1830 is the latest sourced example, not an end date.

sources.quote: Concentric castles resemble one castle nested inside the other, thus creating an inner and outer ward.

period.text: Abroad: Byzantine concentric castles such as Korykos from the early 11th century; the crusader states (1098-1291) built their concentric castles in the 12th and 13th centuries. c. 1000 is approximate.

sources.title: Concentric castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: An example of an early concentric castle is the Byzantine castle of Korykos in Turkey, built in the early 11th century AD.

sources.title: Concentric castle

sources.title: Crusader states

period.text: Medieval and early modern: licences to crenellate were issued from the 12th to the 16th century (the earliest disputed, most surviving from 1199); before around 1600 larger English houses were usually fortified, and in Ireland fortified houses replaced tower houses from the late 16th century to the 1650s. c. 1200 is approximate.

sources.quote: The social, political and military changes that took place from the 1580s-1650s were to play a major role in the development of this unique Irish structure.

types.name: Scottish baronial house

period.text: From the 1560s to about 1660; revived in the 19th century (Abbotsford, rebuilt from 1816), when far more were built than in the first period, the last significant building being the Scottish National War Memorial (opened 1927).

types.plan: often asymmetric, with conical-roofed turrets and battlements

sources.title: Scottish baronial architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The style of elite residences built by barons in Scotland developed under the influence of French architecture and the architecture of the County of Flanders in the 16th century, which had been abandoned by about 1660.

sources.title: Architecture in early modern Scotland
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: From the 1560s great private houses were built in a distinctive style that became known as Scottish Baronial.

sources.title: Scottish baronial architecture

sources.title: Scottish baronial architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The buildings constructed during the Scottish baronial revival by far outnumber those of the original Scottish "baronial" castles of the early modern period.

sources.title: Scottish baronial architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Scottish National War Memorial, opened in 1927 in Edinburgh Castle, was the last significant building in the baronial style.

sources.title: Scottish baronial architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Baronial style buildings were typically of stone, whether ashlar or masonry.

sources.title: Scottish baronial architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: characterised by elaborate rooflines embellished with conical roofs, tourelles, and battlements with machicolations, often with an asymmetric plan

types.name: Bastioned fort

period.text: In England from 1547 (Yarmouth Castle, the first with arrow-head bastions); the bastion system dominated until the first decades of the 19th century and gave way to polygonal forts. c. 1830 is approximate.

types.plan: a fort with projecting bastions

sources.title: Bastion fort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: a style of fortification developed in Italy during the early modern period in response to the ascendancy of gunpowder weapons such as cannon

sources.title: Bastion fort

types.name: Italian bastioned fortification (trace italienne)

period.text: Abroad: developed in Italy in the late 15th and early 16th centuries, spreading out of Italy in the 1530s and 1540s; dominant until the first decades of the 19th century. 1500 and 1830 are approximate.

types.structure: low, thick walls, usually of earth and brick
types.plan: a polygonal curtain wall with pointed bastions at each corner

sources.title: Bastion fort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Bastion fortifications were further developed in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, primarily in response to the French invasion of the Italian peninsula.

sources.title: Bastion fort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The bastion system of fortification had dominated military thinking since its introduction in 16th century Italy, until the first decades of the 19th century.

sources.title: Bastion fort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They were built of many materials, usually earth and brick, as brick does not shatter on impact from a cannonball as stone does.

sources.title: Bastion fort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The design is characterized by a polygonal curtain wall with pointed bastions protruding from each corner.

types.name: Martello tower

period.text: Mostly 1804-1812 in England, Ireland, Jersey and Guernsey; a few later, the last in the British Isles the two at Pembroke Dock (1848-1857).

types.structure: masonry tower about 12 m high with walls about 2.4 m thick, a gun on the flat roof
types.plan: round, two storeys (sometimes over a basement)

sources.title: Martello tower
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland"
sources.quote: Between 1804 and 1812 the British authorities built a chain of towers based on the original Mortella tower to defend the south and east coast of England, Ireland, Jersey and Guernsey

sources.title: Martello tower
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The most notable surviving towers are the two located in Pembroke Dock, which were built between 1848 and 1857 to protect the naval base there.

sources.title: Martello tower
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The towers were about 40 feet (12 m) high with walls about 8 feet (2.4 m) thick.

sources.title: Martello tower
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The interior of a classic British Martello tower consisted of two storeys (sometimes with an additional basement).

types.name: Genoese coastal tower (Corsica)

period.text: Abroad: built by the Republic of Genoa round Corsica between 1530 and 1620, when the programme was abandoned.

types.plan: circular, with a roof terrace protected by machicolations

sources.title: Genoese towers in Corsica
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: are a series of coastal defences constructed by the Republic of Genoa between 1530 and 1620 to stem the attacks by Barbary pirates

sources.title: Genoese towers in Corsica
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Most were built to a similar circular design with a roof terrace protected by machicolations.

types.name: Polygonal fort

period.text: In Britain from the Royal Commission of 1859 (some landward forts at Portsmouth and Plymouth were begun in the 1850s; the Chatham ring not until 1875); the fortifications were completed in the 1880s. c. 1885 is approximate.

types.plan: polygonal, without bastions, the forts placed in a ring to support each other

sources.title: Polygonal fort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The British were apprehensive about a French invasion and in 1859 appointed the Royal Commission on the Defence of the United Kingdom to fortify the naval dockyards of southern England.

sources.title: Royal Commission on the Defence of the United Kingdom
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the time the fortifications were completed in the 1880s it was clear that the French had not seriously planned to invade.

sources.title: Royal Commission on the Defence of the United Kingdom
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Construction of some landward forts at Portsmouth and Plymouth had already begun in the 1850s and work on the ring fortress at Chatham was not started until 1875

sources.title: Royal Commission on the Defence of the United Kingdom
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: These forts were built in the new polygonal style without the traditional bastions and generally sited so as to form a "ring fortress", so that each fort could support its neighbour with artillery fire.

links.claim: Brochs are a complex form of the Iron Age roundhouse.

sources.title: Broch
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Brochs belong to the classification "complex Atlantic roundhouse" devised by Scottish archaeologists in the 1980s.

links.claim: The circular enclosed settlements (rounds) of Cornwall, Devon and south Wales may have shaped the round shell keeps of the Severn region; the usual explanation is the circular earthworks the keeps were built on.

sources.title: Ringfort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the form later influencing the distinctive circular shell-keeps found across the medieval Severnside region

sources.title: Keep
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the major reason for adopting a shell keep design, in the 12th century at least, was the circular design of the original earthworks exploited to support the keep

views: Wikipedia's Ringfort article: the rounds' form influenced the Severnside shell keeps.
Wikipedia's Keep article: shell keeps were circular because the earthworks under them were.

links.claim: Dartmoor and Welsh longhouses were adapted over the 16th and 17th centuries: by 1700 most had separate buildings for livestock, a second storey and a chimney.

sources.title: Longhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: by 1700 most would have been adapted and have separate buildings for livestock, a second storey, stairways, a chimney with bread oven

links.claim: The blackhouse belongs to the North Atlantic longhouse tradition, people and cattle under one roof.

sources.title: Blackhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: As one of the most primitive forms of the North Atlantic longhouse tradition, it is very probable that the roots of the blackhouse, in which cattle and humans shared the same roof, is well over 1000 years old.

links.claim: Bastle houses also keep animals and people in one building, but for defence: animals below, people above.

sources.title: Housebarn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Similarly but for different reasons, some defensive house structures such as the bastle house and some tower houses combine animals on the ground floor and living quarters above, a security measure against raids.

links.claim: The Wealden house is a hall house with jettied two-storey bays at either end of the open hall.

sources.title: Wealden house (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71335)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.

sources.title: Wealden hall house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Wealden hall house is a type of vernacular medieval timber-framed hall house

links.claim: When the open hearth gave way to a chimney, the stack was often built by the cross passage; a stack in the passage leaves a lobby beside it, the plan of the lobby-entry house. The sources describe the insertion and single conversions; none found states the descent of the type as a whole.

sources.title: Hall house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This was created in the vicinity of the cross passage, and sometimes this added chimney actually blocked the cross passage.

sources.title: English vernacular architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The increased use of chimneys and fireplaces meant that the open hall could be ceiled over, creating a house of multiple floors and enclosed rooms.

sources.title: 85 Church Street, Lavenham (Suffolk Heritage Explorer, MSF38224)
sources.author: Suffolk County Council Archaeological Service
sources.quote: A Chimney stack was inserted into the centre of the cross-passage during the 17th century to convert the room into a heated parlour with a newly fashionable 'lobby' entrance

links.claim: In Cumbria the 17th-century plan, one room deep with the entrance through a lobby by the hearth, gave way to the double-pile plan, two rooms deep, in the 18th century.

sources.title: English vernacular architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The main entrance to the house was off the cross passage, through a lobby (mell), separated from the inglenook by a timber partition (heck).

sources.title: English vernacular architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the 18th century, houses moved to a double pile plan, i.e. two rooms deep.

links.claim: Many smaller country houses grew out of medieval hall houses, with rooms added as needed.

sources.title: English country house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: These tend either to have evolved from medieval hall houses, with rooms added as required, or were purpose-built by relatively unknown local architects.

links.claim: Manor houses evolved into country houses, the estate taking the place of the manor.

sources.title: Manor house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: These would eventually evolve into country houses with the estate replacing the manor.

links.claim: The sprawling Elizabethan prodigy houses developed the form of late medieval courtyard houses such as Knole.

sources.title: Prodigy house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the end of the Elizabethan period this sprawling style, essentially developing the form of late medieval buildings like Knole in Kent (which has a total of 7 courtyards), and many Oxbridge colleges, was giving way to more compact high-rising structures

links.claim: The prodigy houses took the Renaissance style mainly from books, French and Flemish decoration more than Italian.

sources.title: Prodigy house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The houses fall within the broad style of Renaissance architecture, but represent a distinctive English take on the style, mainly reliant on books for their knowledge of developments on the Continent.

sources.title: Prodigy house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: French and Flemish Northern Mannerist decoration was more influential than Italian

links.claim: Prodigy houses are the largest and showiest country houses of the Tudor and Jacobean courtiers.

sources.title: Prodigy house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Prodigy houses are large and showy English country houses built by courtiers and other wealthy families

links.claim: A shell keep replaced the palisade on a ringwork (or the timber tower on a motte) with a ring of stone wall.

sources.title: Keep
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: which involved replacing the wooden keep on a motte, or the palisade on a ringwork, with a circular stone wall

links.claim: Shell keeps succeeded motte-and-bailey castles: the timber fence around the top of the motte was replaced by a stone wall.

sources.title: Shell keep
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In English castle morphology, shell keeps are perceived as the successors to motte-and-bailey castles, with the wooden fence around the top of the motte replaced by a stone wall.

links.claim: The first keeps were timber towers on mottes; the Normans then built square stone keeps.

sources.title: Keep
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first keeps were made of timber and formed a key part of the motte-and-bailey castles that emerged in Normandy and Anjou during the 10th century

sources.title: Keep
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Two broad types of design emerged across France and England during the period: four-sided stone keeps, known as Norman keeps or great keeps in English

links.claim: Concentric castles, with two or more rings of walls, were usually built without a free-standing keep.

sources.title: Concentric castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They are typically built without a central free-standing keep.

links.claim: Whether the concentric plan came west from crusader and Byzantine castles is argued over.

sources.title: Concentric castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Some influence from crusader fortification has been conjectured, but the amount of technology transfer from the East and much earlier Byzantine examples remains controversial among historians.

views: Influence from crusader castles has been suggested.
How much passed from the East and from Byzantine examples is disputed.

links.claim: Tower houses are smaller keep-like towers, built from the 14th century by lesser lords while the wealthy built grand keeps.

sources.title: Keep
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: At the same time as these keeps were being built by the extremely wealthy, much smaller, keep-like structures called tower houses or peel towers were built across Ireland, Scotland, and northern England, often by relatively poorer local lords and landowners.

links.claim: In Ireland the tower house may have grown out of the hall house; an older view derived Irish tower houses from Scottish ones.

sources.title: Tower houses in Great Britain and Ireland
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the Irish hall house is in fact the parent of the Irish tower house

sources.title: Keep
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was originally argued that Irish tower houses were based on the Scottish design, but the pattern of development of such castles in Ireland does not support this hypothesis.

sources.title: Tower house (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 68914)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A multi-storey, fortified hall house

views: Tom Finan: the Irish hall house is the parent of the Irish tower house.
Older view: Irish tower houses were based on the Scottish design (not supported by the pattern of development in Ireland).

links.claim: Pele towers are the small tower houses of the Anglo-Scottish border.

sources.title: Peel tower
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Peel towers (also spelt pele) are small fortified keeps or tower houses

links.claim: FISH places the tower house among fortified houses.

sources.quote: A house which bears signs of fortification.

sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A fortified house of two or three storeys

links.claim: The Scottish baronial revival of the 19th century built far more houses in the manner of the old towers than the originals.

sources.title: Scottish baronial architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The buildings constructed during the Scottish baronial revival by far outnumber those of the original Scottish "baronial" castles of the early modern period.

sources.title: Scottish baronial architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: some of the most emblematic country residences of 19th-century Scotland were built in the style, including Queen Victoria's Balmoral Castle and Walter Scott's Abbotsford

links.claim: Henry VIII's Device Forts kept the defences developed for medieval castles while mounting guns.

sources.title: Device Forts
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first wave of work between 1539 and 1543 was characterised by the use of circular bastions and multi-tiered defences, combined with many traditional medieval features.

sources.title: Device Forts
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: defensive paraphernalia developed in the Middle Ages

links.claim: The second phase of the Device Forts (to 1547) brought in angular bastions, probably from Continental thinking.

sources.title: Device Forts
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the second period of construction until 1547 saw the introduction of angular bastions and other innovations probably inspired by contemporary thinking in mainland Europe

links.claim: The bastioned fort was developed in Italy against cannon.

sources.title: Bastion fort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A bastion fort or trace italienne (a phrase derived from non-standard French, meaning 'Italian outline') is a style of fortification developed in Italy

links.claim: Martello towers copied the Genoese tower at Mortella Point in Corsica.

sources.title: Martello tower
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Martello towers were inspired by a round fortress that was part of a larger Genoese defence system at Mortella (Myrtle) Point in Corsica.

links.claim: In the 19th century star-shaped bastioned forts gave way to polygonal forts without bastions.

sources.title: Bastion fort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the nineteenth century, with the development of more powerful artillery and explosive shells, star forts were replaced by simpler but more robust polygonal forts.

sources.title: Polygonal fort
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Unlike earlier forts, polygonal forts had no bastions, which had proven to be vulnerable.
